--- Transcript ---
[Doctor]: Good morning, Mr. Henderson. What brings you into the clinic today?
[Patient]: Good morning, Dr. Vance. Over the last 10 days, I have noticed increasing shortness of breath, especially when climbing stairs or walking more than a block. It feels like a tightness in the center of my chest, like someone is sitting on it, and yesterday I noticed some swelling in both my ankles.
[Doctor]: I understand. Have you had any chest pain that radiates into your jaw, neck, or down your left arm?
[Patient]: Yes, actually, yesterday evening while climbing into bed, the chest heaviness radiated up to the left side of my jaw. It lasted about fifteen minutes and subsided when I sat quietly.
[Doctor]: Any nausea, cold sweats, lightheadedness, or sudden palpitations during those episodes?
[Patient]: I felt slightly nauseous and broke out into a cold sweat during that fifteen-minute spell yesterday. No fainting or passing out, but definitely felt faint.
[Doctor]: Are you currently taking any prescription medications for blood pressure, cholesterol, or blood sugar?
[Patient]: Yes, I take Lisinopril 20 milligrams daily and Atorvastatin 40 milligrams nightly. I was supposed to be taking Metformin 500 milligrams twice daily for prediabetes, but I admit I stopped taking it three months ago because it upset my stomach.
[Doctor]: Thank you for being honest about the Metformin. Any history of heart attacks, bypass surgery, or coronary stents in your immediate family?
[Patient]: My father had a bypass surgery at age 52, and my older brother had a stent placed two years ago at age 58.
[Doctor]: All right. Let's perform a physical examination. Today your seated blood pressure is 148 over 92 millimeters of mercury. Heart rate is 88 beats per minute, regular rhythm. Oxygen saturation is 96 percent on room air. Respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute. Temperature is 98.4 degrees Fahrenheit.
[Doctor]: On examination: Cardiovascular exam shows regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2, but there is an audible S3 gallop at the apex. No murmurs or friction rubs. Pulmonary exam reveals bilateral fine inspiratory crackles at the posterior lung bases extending one-third up. Extremity exam shows bilateral 2-plus pitting pretibial and ankle edema extending to the mid-shins.
[Doctor]: Based on your presentation, symptoms of exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, jaw radiation, S3 gallop, and peripheral edema, I am concerned about acute decompensated heart failure with potential underlying coronary artery ischemia.
[Doctor]: Here is our immediate plan: First, we will obtain an immediate 12-lead electrocardiogram in the clinic room right now to evaluate for acute ischemic changes or ST-segment elevations. Second, we will draw STAT laboratory work including high-sensitivity Troponin I, NT-proBNP, complete blood count, and a comprehensive metabolic panel to assess kidney function and electrolytes.
[Doctor]: Third, we will administer 40 milligrams of oral Furosemide in the clinic to initiate diuresis and reduce preload. Fourth, I will order a STAT transthoracic echocardiogram to assess left ventricular ejection fraction and wall motion abnormalities. Depending on the troponin level and ECG findings, we may transfer you directly to the cardiology observation unit.
